content:
Sam: Heads-up — got a handful of requests about API key UX for project-scoped keys vs org keys. Wanted to sync on runtime checks and migration path.
Maria: +1. Saw some confusion in onboarding: customers create org keys when they meant project keys.
Jordan: Can we do a UI affordance? Default to project-scoped but label org keys as "legacy/global"? :thinking_face:
Lea: UX help is fine but we still need runtime enforcement and a deterministic auth decision path. Right now the runtime treats keys as opaque strings and resolves scope via a db lookup — slightly expensive for hot paths.
Sam: That's the crux. Two orthogonal problems: 1) user-facing semantics / defaults; 2) authn/authz enforcement with perf & audit.
Maria: For enforcement: option A = keep db lookup per request; option B = encode minimal scope in token (signed) to avoid lookup; option C = hybrid with short-lived derived tokens. Tradeoffs?
Jordan: A is simplest for revocation and audit (single source of truth) but adds latency and DB load. B reduces runtime latency but makes revocation harder (need revocation list or short TTL). C tries to get best of both.
Lea: Our serving path target is P50 < 30ms. A synchronous DB hop on the hot path is risky unless cached aggressively. We already have service-level caches, but TTL+staleness semantics matter for revocation windows.
Sam: Practical migration idea: keep canonical API keys (long-lived) in DB. When a key is used, runtime can mint a short-lived signed claim token (derived) that encodes project/org and role. Subsequent requests can use derived token with no DB lookup. Revocation: mark canonical key revoked and push invalidation to cache + derived token revocation list (or short TTL).
Maria: I like the derived token idea. It maps to the dedicated/private deploy model too. How would we surface this to clients? Do we return derived tokens automatically in responses or rotate them via a "session" endpoint?
Jordan: Two approaches: transparent derivation (runtime returns a Set-Cookie-like header or an X-Auth-Derived header) or explicit exchange endpoint (POST /v1/auth/exchange -> gives derived token). Transparent helps existing clients with no change, but it's weird for REST semantics.
Lea: From a security perspective, explicit exchange is nicer. It forces clients to use an auth flow and we can rate-limit/monitor exchange. Also lets us record the origin that created the derived token.
Sam: Agreed. Proposed flow: client presents API key -> runtime checks canonical key -> returns 201 with derived token and expires_in. Client caches and uses derived token for subsequent requests. We should default derived TTL to 5m for interactive, 1m for high-volume paths, configurable per route.
Maria: TTL variability per route makes sense and maps to our Optimize suggestions. Implement runtime config: route-level auth policy with derived_ttl and cache_invalidation hooks.
Jordan: Implementation detail: derived token format — JWT-ish with minimal claims: sub=key-id, scope=[project:123], roles=[ingest], iat, exp, sig. Use our existing signing key per-region. No nested claims beyond arrays.
Lea: Also need fast revocation: we can maintain a Redis blacklist of revoked derived token jti for the short TTL; since TTL is small blacklist size is bounded. For canonical key revocation we flush cached derived tokens via pubsub invalidation to runtime nodes.
Sam: Good. Observability: every exchange should emit an event with key-id, requester-ip, route, and reason. Important for audit and for anomaly detection. Maria — can product/console surface derived-token issuance metrics?
Maria: Yes, Console can show exchanges and per-key issuance rate. We'll add an affordance: flag in key settings to "Allow derived tokens" default true for new project keys, false for org keys during migration.
Jordan: Migration concerns: existing clients might be using org keys widely. Plan: step 1) introduce derived-token exchange endpoint and console defaults; step 2) instrument and opt-in org keys for derivation for a trial; step 3) make project keys default; step 4) eventually deprecate org-key creation for new orgs. All while supporting revocation.
Lea: One more runtime optimization: keep a tiny LRU map of (api-key-hash -> resolved-scope + key-id) in memory per runtime worker to avoid Redis/DB for cold derived-token exchange calls. Persist canonical store in primary DB. Eviction policy size tuned by worker memory footprint.
Sam: Sounds good. On introspection vs self-contained: introspection endpoints are heavy. Our exchange-derived model gives self-contained tokens with short TTL so introspection isn't needed normally. But we should offer an introspection endpoint for long-lived canonical key metadata / for third-party integrations.
Maria: Audit log requirements: record both canonical key ops (create, rotate, revoke) and derived token exchanges. Also add a console filter to view exchanges by project and by IP.
Jordan: Danger: offline jobs that run long (backfills) will not like short derived TTL. Option: allow jobs to request "long-lived exchange" with proof-of-intent (e.g., via job registration + admin grant) which returns a longer-lived derived token bound to host fingerprint and limited scopes. Needs careful ops review.
Lea: Agree — whitelist flow for long-lived job tokens. Track via admin audit and require HMAC binding to machine ID.
Sam: Action items: 1) Lea + Jordan prototype runtime LRU + derived-token path (spike) — target EOD next Wed. 2) Maria to add console UX mock for key settings + exchange metrics — wireframe by next Tues. 3) Sam to draft one-pager for migration plan and security review.
dev-bot: Reminder: assigned tasks recorded in GH issue #4102.
Sam: Thanks. Any strong objections to the derived-token + explicit exchange approach?
Maria: None from product side.
Jordan: No blockers. Need to confirm signing key rotation behavior — derived tokens must survive key rotation window or be invalidated safely.
Lea: We'll include key-rotation semantics in the spike — plan: sign derived tokens with a short-lived signing key rotated frequently; on rotation, runtimes accept previous key for grace window and we force-exchange tokens older than rotation if needed.
Sam: OK — let's reconvene after the spike. I'll drop the one-pager draft in #eng-security later today. :slightly_smiling_face:
